Donald McLeod again

Another composition by Pipe Major Donald McLeod, but he never wrote it in G, and I’ve never heard it played in that key, anywhere.
The name refers not to a bird, but to a piper of Donald’s acquaintance who had an odd posture when he was playing.

Alternative version

X:3, broadly the same as X:2 from my colleague DonaldK, is from a sheet handed out at a workshop, and although the main differences are rhythmic there are a few different notes and a 2nd-time ending for strain 2.

The story I have is that only strains 1 & 2 are by Pipe Major Donald MacLeod, and that 3 & 4 were added by piper Willie “Wulls” Galbraith - to good effect, as DonaldK observes.

The Duck, X:4

Previous settings were 4-parts. The A & C parts were almost identical in X1, aside from a few alternatives notes in the the bar (which harmonized). The B & D parts differed a bit more, but, could be played simultaneously without any issues, since they harmonize.

The Duck, X:6

This is Donald MacLeod’s own setting, with the Highland pipe ornaments left out, and short trills (praltriller/schneller/inverted mordent) put in to try to capture the way the tune sounds on the pipes.

The effect of the repeated D’s in the second part is, I think, critical to the sound of the tune.

There’s a pipe-specific thing that happens in the second part: the high A which follows the low A in Bar 1 disappears into the drones, making the low A sound detached.

This tune is the second jig in a three-jig set on the biggest-selling bagpipe album of all time, Farewell To The Greys (1971). The set of jigs is:

Groatie Buckie Mannie
The Duck
Eleanor’s

I’ve posted the first and third jigs because they weren’t in Tunes.

On the album that set of jigs is part of a larger medley:

1) Leaving Rhu Vaternish (slow air)
2) Groatie Buckie Mannie (called “nameless” on the album)
3) The Duck
4) Eleanor’s
5) Drum Salute (drum corps only)

Re: The Duck

I understand this tune, “The Duck”, was originally written about a regimental piper who had a particular stance and way of walking when playing, so nicknamed “The Duck”. I’ll see if I can find the source of that anecdote, but I suspect either the Scots Guards or The Queen’s Own Highlanders.

UPDATE:
The tunes is in Donald MacLeod’s 4th collection ( he composed it) and in the Caberfeidh Collection of The Queen’s Own Highlanders- Seaforths and Camerons, which is where I saw the backstory, if I remember correctly.
